title: The Rundown
full_review:
����������� A brawny bounty hunter gets more than he bargained for when he takes on an assignment deep in the Amazon jungle in director Peter Berg's sporadically entertaining action-comedy "The Rundown" (Universal).

Trading in his "Scorpion King" sandals for some mosquito repellent, Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson plays Beck, a supersized leg-breaker whose aptitude for destruction is reined in by a cool-headed pacifist bent. What Beck really wants is to be a restaurateur (don't ask), so when his loan shark boss -- to whom he is vaguely in debt -- offers to wipe his slate clean and set him up with his own bistro in exchange for one last job, Beck signs up.

Now if Johnson had spent a little less time in the ring smashing people over the head with chairs and watched more movies, he would have known that it's always that "one last job" that gets you in trouble. The quarry in question is Travis (Seann William Scott), a smart-aleck treasure hunter who has discovered the location of a priceless Mayan artifact deep in the jungles of Brazil.

Travis also happens to be the son of Beck's employer; apparently, Travis slept with the wrong man's wife and Daddy wants him to come home and face the disciplinary music. Beck nets Travis without breaking a sweat, but his easy exit is stymied by Hatcher (Christopher Walken), a kooky despot who runs the local gold mine -- a hellhole out of Dante's Inferno, which "employs" the indigenous population as slave labor. Hatcher wants to keep Travis in the country long enough for him to recover the valuable idol from its secret hiding place in the rain forest.

Beck and Travis manage to escape, but find themselves lost in the wilds without a map -- or, for that matter, much of a script. Despite good on-screen chemistry between Johnson and Scott, the brain-and-beefcake buddy film unravels into steroid-enhanced-fish-out-of-water slapstick silliness, including an encounter with oversexed killer monkeys.

Along the way they are captured by a band of guerrilla rebels, led by a local beauty, Marianna (Rosario Dawson). She offers them safe passage to the airstrip where Beck's plane is waiting. In return, she demands that they first help her obtain the golden statuette Travis was looking for, which she intends to sell in order to raise enough money to free the mineworkers.

From here, the already threadbare narrative nosedives into a WWF production of "Raiders of the Lost Ark" -- or in this case "Raiders of the Lost Plot," pitting the smack-talking treasure hunters against Hatcher's goons, leading to the film's predictable high-octane showdown.

Johnson injects a refreshing charm and humor into what is essentially a two-note, smash-and-sulk role. However, sporadic inane references to porcini mushrooms do not a three-dimensional character make. And while the part proves that Johnson can flex more than just his biceps, his choice of material is a bit rocky. Walken, who is making a second career out of self-parody, lends his quirky brand of oddball absurdity to what amounts to a plot place-holder performance.

Throughout the film Beck -- a combination of Gandhi and the Terminator -- exhibits a Zen-like aversion to violence, eschewing brute force for reasoned discussion. Yet the peaceful philosophy to which he subscribes is little more than lip service, a cleverly scripted smokescreen to amp up the applause when his inner ticking time-bomb finally explodes, unleashing his pyrotechnic fury. And while it does suggest several lame violence-is-bad public service announcements throughout the carnage, Beck's path of least resistance leads to the same old Hollywood destination: Mayhem, U.S.A.

A running joke has Beck offering those unfortunate enough to cross him a multiple-choice of options: a) the painless way sans force, and b) well, you get the picture. Moviegoers are faced with a similar menu: a) fork over money to see yet another painful exercise in excess, or b) save your cash. Take some advice: Choose b.

Due to recurring action violence and some crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
